source: Richter and de Lange (2019) Statistical learning attenuates visual activity only for attended stimuli (eLife)
url: https://elifesciences.org/articles/47869 (full text via Europe PMC PMC6731093)
finding: Expectation suppression in ventral visual cortex appeared only when participants attended the object images. It vanished when they attended letters at fixation. Learned pairs still gave behavioural benefits.
numbers: N=34 (df 33), whole-brain fMRI, learned object pairs. Suppression when attended: V1 t(33)=3.573 p=0.001. Expectation x attention interaction: V1 F(1,33)=7.706 p=0.009 eta2=0.189; LOC F=12.580 p=0.001 eta2=0.276; TOFC F=16.955 p=2.4e-4 eta2=0.339. Behaviour interaction RT F(1,33)=37.543 p=6.6e-7.
quote: expectation suppression was only evident when objects were attended and vanished when participants attended the concurrently presented alphanumeric characters
limits: One lab, one paradigm (object pairs, two days training). Predictive coding can still argue attention boosts error gain; the authors say so. Does not show attention alone explains suppression.
agent_relevance: Error signals may be gated by attention. For a scaffold: surprise checks only help on content the agent is actually attending to. Background only.

source: Alink and Blank (2021) Can expectation suppression be explained by reduced attention to predictable stimuli? (NeuroImage 231:117824)
finding: Perspective piece. Argues expectation suppression may reflect reduced saliency-driven attention to predictable stimuli, not reduced prediction error. Cites Richter and de Lange 2019 as the main challenge. Lists studies with better decoding for UNexpected stimuli (Jiang 2013, Kumar 2017, Richter 2018, Tang 2018). Proposes orthogonal manipulation of probability and saliency, decoding, laminar 7T, EEG/MEG timing.
numbers: No new data and no sample sizes. Evidence for the attention account rests mainly on Richter and de Lange 2019 (N=34).
limits: Not an experiment. Predictive coding can absorb the result by letting attention scale error precision. So the question (does attention EXPLAIN suppression) is an open competing explanation, not settled.
agent_relevance: Confirms the K06 caveat: expectation suppression alone does not prove error coding. Background only.

source: Feuerriegel, Vogels and Kovacs (2021) Evaluating the evidence for expectation suppression in the visual system (Neurosci Biobehav Rev 124)
finding: Names four confounds in expectation suppression work: surprise, attention, repetition/adaptation, novelty. Genuine suppression found only in a subset of statistical-learning designs with weeks of sequence learning before measurement. Designs where probabilities were learned in 1-2 sessions gave inconsistent evidence.
numbers: No pooled effect size in the abstract. Designs reviewed: probabilistic cueing, statistical learning, oddball, action-outcome, apparent motion.
quote: inconsistent evidence for genuine expectation suppression
limits: Abstract only read; full text not open access. Narrative review, not a meta-analysis.
agent_relevance: Process-theory support is conditional on long learning. Do not cite single-session expectation suppression as proof.

source: Yan, Ehinger, Perez-Bellido, Peelen and de Lange (2023) Humans predict the forest, not the trees (Cerebral Cortex 33:8300)
finding: Post-2021 fMRI study. Temporal expectation suppression in LOC occurred only for whole learned 4-object displays, not for single objects within mixed or shuffled displays. No effect in V1 or PPA.
numbers: N=34 (35 recruited). LOC familiar displays t(33)=-3.44 p<0.01 dz=-0.60; mixed BF10=0.19; shuffled BF10=0.25; omnibus display x expectation only P=0.06. V1 no effects. Object level in mixed displays LOC t(33)=1.55 p=0.13 BF10=0.54. Behaviour: 905 vs 931 ms, t(33)=-3.48.
limits: Search snippet said the study was preregistered on OSF; not opened to confirm. Not a direct replication of an earlier study. Does not test sharpening vs dampening.
agent_relevance: Prediction effects sit at the level of learned wholes, which fits a hierarchy; weak single-object effects argue against cheap, universal error signals.

source: Rideaux, Hu, Chidley, Cloos, Schwarzkopf and Mattingley (2026) A comparison of sharpening and dampening accounts of the role of expectation in shaping neural fidelity of early visual cortex (preprint)
finding: fMRI pRF mapping plus EEG inverted encoding. The apparent expectancy effect was better explained by local spatiotemporal stimulus properties than by global expectancy. Pattern resembled adaptation, but fit best an expectation of temporal stability plus dampening (response and fidelity both suppressed).
numbers: Abstract has no N or effect sizes.
quote: predictive processing may operate through dampening
limits: Preprint, abstract only; post hoc EEG analysis. Single study.
agent_relevance: Opposite sign to Kok 2012 sharpening. The 'prior makes representations cleaner' story is contested.

source: Kok, Jehee and de Lange (2012) Less is more: expectation sharpens representations in the primary visual cortex (Neuron 75:265)
finding: fMRI plus MVPA in V1: expectation lowered response amplitude but improved stimulus decoding. Improvement independent of task relevance (attention). Correlated with behavioural improvement when feature was relevant.
numbers: Not in abstract (original N and decoding accuracies not read).
quote: expectation facilitates perception by sharpening sensory representations
limits: Abstract only. Later studies cited by Alink and Blank 2021 (Jiang 2013, Kumar 2017, Richter 2018, Tang 2018) found better decoding for unexpected stimuli; Rideaux 2026 favours dampening. No close independent replication of the sharpening result was found.
agent_relevance: Sharpening claim is not reliably replicated; do not build on it.

source: Rao and Ballard (1999) Predictive coding in the visual cortex (Nature Neuroscience 2:79-87)
finding: Model: feedback carries predictions, feedforward carries residual errors. Trained on natural images, a hierarchical network developed simple-cell-like receptive fields; error units showed endstopping and other extra-classical effects.
numbers: Methods numbers (patch size, units, image count) NOT read: paper is paywalled; only the abstract and page header (5613 citations) were visible.
quote: feedforward connections carry the residual errors between the predictions and the actual lower-level activities
limits: Model only; shows plausibility, not that cortex does it. Alternatives (sparse coding, normalisation) can also produce endstopping.
agent_relevance: Origin of the residual-only idea; no direct LLM test.

source: Murray, Kersten, Olshausen, Schrater and Woods (2002) Shape perception reduces activity in human primary visual cortex (PNAS 99:15164)
finding: fMRI: grouped shapes raised LOC activity and lowered V1 activity versus randomly arranged elements. Read as higher areas explaining away lower-level input. Note: the gap list says Murray 2004; this 2002 paper is the one with the V1/LOC effect.
numbers: Abstract has no N or percent signal change. Full text scan not retrievable (PMC render and PNAS PDF blocked).
limits: Abstract only. Grouping and attention confounds are possible.

source: Heilbron, Armeni, Schoffelen, Hagoort and de Lange (2022) A hierarchy of linguistic predictions during natural language comprehension (PNAS 119)
finding: GPT-2 predictions explain brain responses during audiobooks. Separate prediction dimensions (syntactic category, phonemes, semantics) have dissociable neural signatures. Word-level predictions inform phoneme-level ones. Nearest multi-level language test found; no newer test with 3+ levels (syntax, semantics, discourse) was found in this session.
numbers: EEG: 19 participants, 1 h. MEG: 3 individuals, 9 h, head casts. Continuous prediction vs constrained guessing t(18)=3.18 p=5.2e-3; prediction vs baseline t(18)=5.01 p=9.04e-5.
limits: Only 3 MEG participants. Levels are syntax category, word, phoneme, semantics; no discourse level. Predictions come from GPT-2, so the transfer-vs-prediction confound (Antonello and Huth) applies. Search coverage for newer work was weak because APIs were rate limited.
agent_relevance: Supports layered prediction in language, but gives no operator for the scaffold.

source: Ma et al. (2024) Non-myopic generation of language models for reasoning and planning (Predictive-Decoding): math and equal-compute rows
finding: Foresight resampling beats plain decoding on math. Beam search gives similar gains but needs over 3x the compute. Combining with self-consistency helps a little more.
numbers: Llama-3 8B: GSM8K +7.2, MATH +4.3; Mistral-0.3 7B: +13.3, +6.8. One readable Mistral GSM8K row: self-consistency (8 samples) 80.9 vs Predictive-Decoding+SC 81.3. Table text extraction is garbled, pairings approximate.
limits: Gain over equal-budget self-consistency is about 0.4 points in the readable row. Best-of-N at equal tokens not cleanly separated.
agent_relevance: Foresight is a planning operator, not PC. Its edge over equal-budget voting is small on math.

source: Ma et al. (2024) Predictive-Decoding: code and agent tables (HumanEval, MBPP, AlfWorld, PDDL)
finding: Foresight resampling also helps on code and agent planning, not only math. On Llama-3 code it beats beam search at about a quarter of the FLOPs. Agent success rates rise a lot.
numbers: Llama-3 8B HumanEval pass@1: autoregressive 44.3, beam 53.5 (290e12 FLOPs), self-infilling 51.8, Predictive-Decoding 57.3 (76.6e12). MBPP pass@1 33.5 vs 38.4. DeepSeek-Coder 6.7B HumanEval 45.2 vs 47.6. AlfWorld Llama-3.1 70B success: Act 19.4, ReAct 18.7, PD 44.0. PDDL: Act 35.0, PD 38.3. GPT-3.5 AlfWorld: ReAct 7.5, PD 14.9.
limits: Fixed benchmark suite. PD FLOPs on the 70B agent runs are very large (224.1e13), so agent gains are not at equal cost. No non-verifiable tasks (writing, forecasting).
agent_relevance: Gap 2 partly closed: holds on code and agent tasks; untested on open-ended tasks; equal-cost evidence mixed.

source: Bhatt et al. (2026) PCIB: Predictive Coding and Information Bottleneck hallucination detection
finding: Full text read. Evaluation is HaluBench n=200 only; no confidence intervals, bootstrap or cross-validation described. The comparison with Lynx (87.4% accuracy, 70B, 15,000 training samples) mixes AUROC with accuracy.
numbers: AUROC: theory-guided 0.8017 (unsupervised); base RF 0.8274; improved RF 0.8669; meta-ensemble 0.8414 base and 0.8458 improved. Simple averaging 0.48. Claimed +4.95%; arithmetic is +3.95 points. Rationalization signal: negative result.
limits: N=200, one benchmark, no CI, authors only. 'Predictive coding' is a label for context-adherence features, not a PC implementation.
agent_relevance: Gap 3 stays open: no larger-N or multi-benchmark replication found. Weak lead.

source: Innocenti, Achour and Buckley (2025) muPC: Scaling Predictive Coding to 100+ Layer Networks
finding: Depth-muP parameterisation lets PC residual networks train stably to 128 layers with little tuning and zero-shot learning-rate transfer across width and depth. Fixes only some instabilities. Simple classification tasks; no language-model or transformer experiment mentioned.
numbers: 128 layers max. Abstract page gives no accuracy or parameter count.
quote: a first step towards scaling PC to more complex architectures
limits: Abstract page only. With Pinchetti 2022 (small transformer, 590.08 vs 162.64 ppl) there is no evidence PC LMs scale past 100M parameters.
agent_relevance: Gap 8: PC training at LLM size is unshown, not shown impossible. Irrelevant to a prompt scaffold.

source: Huang et al. (2024) Large Language Models Cannot Self-Correct Reasoning Yet (ICLR 2024)
finding: Without oracle labels, intrinsic self-correction gives no gain and often hurts. Gains in earlier work came from oracle stopping.
numbers: GPT-3.5 GSM8K 75.9 -> 75.1 (round 1) -> 74.7 (round 2); CommonSenseQA 75.8 -> 38.1 -> 41.8; HotpotQA 26.0 -> 25.0. GPT-4 GSM8K 95.5 -> 91.5 -> 89.0; CommonSenseQA 82.0 -> 79.5 -> 80.0. With oracle: GPT-3.5 GSM8K 95.5, GPT-4 97.5.
limits: 2023 models; prompt design matters (their own point). Verifiable-answer tasks.
agent_relevance: Gap 9: a PC-style predict-compare-update loop built only from model self-feedback must beat this null. Needs an external or verifier signal.

source: Huang et al. (2024) multi-agent debate vs self-consistency, same paper
finding: Critique-and-revise by several model copies does not beat plain majority voting at equal number of responses.
numbers: GSM8K (gpt-3.5): standard 76.7; self-consistency 3 responses 82.5, 6 -> 85.3, 9 -> 88.2; debate at 9 responses about 83.0 (table columns garbled; debate is below SC at 9).
limits: One model family and dataset; table layout garbled in text extraction.
agent_relevance: Any new operator (including residual passing) must be compared with self-consistency at equal calls.

source: Olausson et al. (2024) Is Self-Repair a Silver Bullet for Code Generation? (ICLR 2024)
finding: At equal sample budget, self-repair gives modest, uneven gains, sometimes none. The bottleneck is feedback quality. Better feedback (stronger model or human) helps a lot. More initial samples matter more than more repairs.
numbers: GPT-4 on APPS: 10 initial + 1 repair each (20 total) = 1.05x pass@20; 2 initial + 10 repairs (22) = 0.97x pass@22. Human feedback raised repair success 33.3% -> 52.6% (1.58x). Code Llama gains up to 10% vs baseline; GPT-3.5 up to 3%.
limits: Code with unit tests; repair gets full program plus error, not a minimal delta. No test of delta-only passing.
agent_relevance: Gap 1 stays open: no study isolates delta-only vs full re-read at equal tokens. Closest evidence says feedback quality, not format, decides the gain.

source: Huang (2025) Feature selective inhibitory mechanisms enable expectation suppression in cortical microcircuits
finding: Circuit model with pyramidal, PV, SOM and VIP cells: SOM cells suppress predicted inputs by feature-specific dendritic inhibition; VIP disinhibits for unexpected inputs. A mechanism for expectation suppression compatible with error units.
limits: Simulation, abstract only, cited once. A model showing it can work is not evidence cortex does it.

source: Richter and de Lange (2019) behaviour and pupil results, same study as d01
finding: Expected objects were categorised faster and more accurately when attended; the behavioural benefit interacted with attention. Pupil dilation (a surprise/arousal proxy) raised V1 BOLD whether or not images were expected.
numbers: Accuracy interaction F(1,33)=5.203 p=0.029 eta2=0.136; RT F(1,33)=37.543 p=6.6e-7 eta2=0.532. Pupil N=32: no expectation interaction (F(1,31)=2.261 p=0.143).
limits: Same study as d01; one source, not independent.
agent_relevance: Arousal and attention are rival explanations to rule out when claiming a surprise signal helps.
